frameworks.name: 10-Chessboard Leverage Principle
frameworks.definition: Every marketing action, dollar, or resource deployed should simultaneously generate content or reach across at least 10 channels, so each move compounds rather than spending once.

claims.text: Greg Lavecchia (Bloom, co-founder CEO) asserts that in the leverage economy (2026 framing), every marketing action should be designed to play on at least 10 channels simultaneously rather than executing a single-channel event. The mechanism is that any real-world activation can be repurposed into content distributed across multiple social platforms, multiplying the return on a fixed resource investment.
claims.speaker: Greg Lavecchia
conditions: businesses with social media distribution capability
claims.mechanism: A single real-world event generates authentic content assets (video, photo, crowd reaction) that can be deployed across 10 or more social channels, converting one fixed-cost activation into the equivalent of 10 independent campaigns.
bounded_by: Does not apply to single-channel-only brands without content capture or distribution infrastructure

claims.text: Greg Lavecchia (Bloom) argues that in-real-life sampling events (e.g., grocery store canvassing) are not worth doing unless the event is simultaneously captured as content and distributed across at least 10 social channels. Without content capture, the ROI of a physical event is confined to that single activation, making it economically uncompetitive versus digital-first approaches.
claims.speaker: Greg Lavecchia
claims.speaker_term: go get cans in hands, go do samplings
conditions: consumer packaged goods or physical product brands
claims.mechanism: Without content capture, a sampling event spends its budget once with local reach only; with content capture and multi-channel deployment, the same spend reaches a geographically unconstrained digital audience multiplying effective impressions.
bounded_by: Does not apply to events where content capture is legally or operationally impossible

claims.text: Greg Lavecchia (Bloom) claims that geographic origin of a real-world marketing event is irrelevant to its digital distribution value: a London product-sampling event can generate content used effectively for American marketing audiences, because social media distribution is not geographically constrained to where the event occurred.
claims.speaker: Greg Lavecchia
conditions: content captured at the event is platform-appropriate for target market
bounded_by: Does not apply when local regulatory or cultural context makes cross-market repurposing irrelevant or misleading

examples.text: Greg Lavecchia (Bloom) describes running a product-sampling event in the center of London where people lined up down the street to receive product. Rather than treating this as a local UK activation, Bloom captured content from the event and deployed it in American marketing campaigns. The London event functioned simultaneously as a brand moment in the UK and as content inventory for the US market, illustrating the 10-chessboard principle: one real-world event played on more than one geographic chessboard at once.

practices.text: Before executing any in-real-life marketing event (sampling, activation, pop-up), ensure a content capture plan is in place so the event generates distributable assets for at least 10 social channels. If no content capture plan exists, reconsider whether the event is worth the investment.
Evaluate every marketing dollar deployed by asking how many channels or chessboards it can simultaneously reach; reject single-channel-only spend in favor of multi-channel-amplifiable activations.
